outcome: Under the standard definition (triples {p, p+2, p+6} or {p, p+4, p+6}) the infinitude of prime triplets is still open, and no event since 26 January 2024 addresses it: the in-window items are bounds on prime pairs (bounded gaps, with AI-linked claims at 246 formalised, 240, 236, 212 and 186), an almost-prime or conditional triple result, a constellation computation, a twin-prime preprint with a failing key step, and an AI-linked large-gap claim. A pre-window positive-proportion theorem of Maynard (arXiv 2013, Annals 2015) yields, by a pigeonhole step I supply, infinitely many prime triples of some admissible shape, which answers a broader reading of the bullet but not the standard forms.
problem_asks: The bullet asks one existence question: whether there are infinitely many prime triplets. It does not define 'prime triplet', so the parts are: (a) Standard reading (Wikipedia 'Prime triplet'; Hardy and Wright 1979): sets of three primes of the form {p, p+2, p+6} or {p, p+4, p+6}; the bullet asks whether there are infinitely many such sets. The bullet does not say whether both forms are needed or whether an infinite family of either form suffices; an infinite family of one form would already make the bullet's answer yes under this reading. (b) Broad reading: infinitely many n for which all of n+h1, n+h2, n+h3 are prime for some admissible triple (h1,h2,h3) of integers, with the shape not fixed. (c) Strict reading used in some problem-solving sources (AoPS wiki): three primes in arithmetic progression with common difference 2, under which only {3,5,7} qualifies. Nothing in the bullet asks about bounds, dimensions, or any quantity other than the count of triples. Note that Hardy-Littlewood predicts the count of standard triples below x grows like C x/(log x)^3, but the bullet does not ask for the asymptotic.

events.what_happened: Shan-Guang Tan, 'On the solution of the Collatz problem', arXiv:1110.3465 (math.GM). The paper's abstract claims a proof of the Collatz problem (quoted by the fetch as: each Collatz sequence always returns to 1, i.e., the Collatz problem is solved). A search summary of the PDF reports a 'Prime triplet theorem' (Section 55 in that summary) asserting infinitely many (p, p+2, p+6) triples, argued from a lower bound for twin primes. I opened only the arXiv abstract page, which says nothing about prime triplets; I did not read the section.

events.delivers: Claimed but unverified: infinitude of (p, p+2, p+6) triples, via a twin-prime lower bound that the claim uses as an input. Restriction: the form is the standard one, and the argument depends on the twin-prime input.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, unless the triplet section is accepted. I found no acceptance.
events.doubts: Single-author claim in math.GM. The triplet theorem, as summarised, rests on a lower bound for twin primes, which is itself unproven and is the input the bullet's neighbouring problems need. The search summary found no sign of peer review or acceptance. The section text was not verified by me.

events.what_happened: James Maynard, 'Small gaps between primes', arXiv:1311.4600 (v1 19 Nov 2013); published in Annals of Mathematics 181 (2015). The abstract, as fetched, says: 'for each k, the prime k-tuples conjecture holds for a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples'. A rendering of the main statement (Theorem 1.2), obtained from an automated summary of the ar5iv HTML because my fetch of the arXiv PDF returned only compressed binary, reads: for fixed m and r sufficiently large in terms of m, and a set of r distinct integers, the number of m-element subsets with infinitely many n such that all n+h_i are prime is at least a constant (depending on m) times the number of m-element subsets. The rendering shows no admissibility hypothesis, but one must be present, since a non-admissible subset cannot have all of its translates prime. I could not verify the rendering against the primary text. The same paper gives bounded gaps (H1 at most 600).
events.revisions: arXiv v1 19 Nov 2013; v3 28 Oct 2019 (latest per the arXiv abstract page). Journal version Annals of Mathematics 181 (2015), listing seen in search, not opened.
events.delivers: For m = 3 this gives, for a suitable large set, a positive proportion of its 3-element subsets for which infinitely many translates consist entirely of primes. By a pigeonhole step (my inference; no source I read states it): some specific admissible triple has infinitely many n with n+h1, n+h2, n+h3 all prime, so there are infinitely many prime triples of some admissible shape. The shape is not specified; nothing in the statement singles out (0,2,6) or (0,4,6). Restrictions: m fixed, set size large in terms of m, and admissibility as the paper imposes it.
events.remains: On the standard forms {p, p+2, p+6} and {p, p+4, p+6}, nothing: the statement does not name either. On the broad reading, nothing remains, on my inference.

disputes.summary: Source tension on the broad reading. Wikipedia's Prime k-tuple article says there is no tuple for which the conjecture has been proven except the trivial 1-tuple (0). Maynard's 2013 positive-proportion theorem (as rendered), the Mor-Gupta 2024 claim and the pigeonhole consequence of Maynard-Tao together imply that some admissible triple has infinitely many all-prime translates. The two cannot both hold on the same reading. Not resolved here; the judging pass must choose the reading.
Mor and Gupta (2024) claim a positive-proportion result for each k, in wording matching the abstract of Maynard's 2013 paper. The novelty claim is unclear and I could not read their full text.

Bounded-gap records (pairs; not triples) were claimed within weeks: Stadlmann 240 (31 Aug 2026), OpenAI 186 (PDF dated 30 Aug 2026, announced about 3 Sep), Axiom 212 (3 Sep 2026), Song-Yue 236 (ePrint approved 9 Sep 2026), against Polymath8b 246 (2014, with Axiom's 246 formalisation Aug 2026). The registry treats the question of whether 212 supersedes 246 as an open editorial matter and says the 186 claim does not displace it on the evidence. Who did the OpenAI 186 mathematics. The paper is listed under 'OpenAI' alone (secondary report). 'GPT-6 Astra' is named by Weijie Su's post (search snippet) and aggregator pages, and the Wikipedia AI list uses 'OpenAI'. The authors' own text was unreadable to me, so the model's role is unverified.

summary: I ran 38 searches and opened about 25 pages; several primary PDFs were unreadable through my tools and quotes from some pages come through a summarising fetch, so verbatim wording is not guaranteed where I say so. Under the standard definition (Wikipedia's Prime triplet article: {p, p+2, p+6} or {p, p+4, p+6}), I found no in-window event that addresses the infinitude of these triples. The in-window items are: bounded-gap claims on prime pairs (Axiom's formalisation of 246, 17 Aug 2026; Stadlmann 240; OpenAI 186; Axiom 212; Song-Yue 236); an almost-prime or conditional triple result (de la Breteche, Oct 2024; Volfson, Jan and Mar 2026); a computation on constellations of length 459 (Holt, Mar 2026, with a sequel in May); an unrefereed twin-prime preprint whose key inference fails (Cambridge, Jul-Aug 2026); and an AI-linked large-gap claim (GPT-5.6 Sol, Aug 2026). The question moves in the pre-window literature. Maynard's positive-proportion theorem (arXiv Nov 2013; Annals 2015) states that for fixed m and a large set, a positive proportion of m-subsets have infinitely many all-prime translates. Applied to m = 3 with a pigeonhole step, which is my inference and not stated in any source I read, it gives some admissible triple with infinitely many prime translates, but it names no shape, so the standard forms are not reached. Polymath8b (July 2014) gives, conditionally on the generalised Elliott-Halberstam hypothesis, only 'at least two' primes among any admissible triple. The Wikipedia Prime k-tuple article says no tuple has been proven except the 1-tuple, which conflicts with the broad reading; I could not resolve that conflict. Mor and Gupta (Baghdad Science Journal, 2024) claim the positive-proportion statement for each k, unconditionally, but I could not read the full text. Tan's 2011 Collatz paper has a claimed 'prime triplet theorem' that rests on a twin-prime input and is unverified; I did not read its section. On AI: no AI-attributed result I found touches triples. The AI-linked in-window items are all pair-gap or large-gap claims. Axiom's Lean formalisation of the 246 theorem is formalisation of existing mathematics. For Axiom's 212 claim the registry says AxiomProver produced the Lean certificate and that the mathematics is the humans'. For OpenAI's 186 claim the paper is credited to 'OpenAI' and 'GPT-6 Astra' is named only by secondary posts, and I could not read the authors' PDF. None of these enters ai.systems: for Axiom 246 the role was formalisation, and for Axiom 212 and OpenAI 186 I could not obtain an authors' quote showing the system's load-bearing role. I could not find any primary source for the DeepMind 'hidden pattern in prime numbers' video (May and June 2026). Close calls: (1) whether the bullet means the standard forms or any admissible triple, which its wording leaves open; (2) whether Maynard's theorem has the hypothesis I think it has, since I could only read a rendering; (3) whether the Mor-Gupta claim adds anything to Maynard.
competing_reading: The strongest case for the broad reading: the bullet says 'prime triplets' without naming the forms, and Maynard's 2013 theorem with the pigeonhole step gives infinitely many prime triples of some admissible shape. On that reading the question was answered in 2013-2015, and the in-window record should say that the bullet is already settled and nothing in the window bears on it. The case against: the standard usage (the Wikipedia Prime triplet article, Hardy and Wright) names two forms and calls the infinitude open, the Prime k-tuple article says no tuple is proven, and Maynard's result names no shape, so it cannot be applied to (0,2,6) or (0,4,6). A reader could also take the Mor-Gupta claim, if it were stronger than Maynard, as a route to a specific shape, but the abstract as summarised does not say so.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The exact hypotheses of Maynard's Theorem 1.2 in the Annals text: admissibility of the set, the m = 3 case, and the quantifier over subsets. (2) A statement in print by a number theorist on whether Maynard-Tao settles the broad reading (none found). (3) Any argument that gives infinitely many (p, p+2, p+6) or (p, p+4, p+6) triples (none found). (4) The Mor-Gupta full text and its first public date. (5) The OpenAI PDF and Axiom's bgp212.pdf, for the authors' own account of AI roles. (6) Tan's Section 55 text and whether the claim appears in any refereed venue.
